content: Hydrocortisone (rectal) is a corticosteroid with anti-inflammatory properties. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of inflamed hemorrhoids, post-radiation proctitis, chronic ulcerative colitis, cryptitis, pruritus ani, and other inflammatory conditions of the anorectal region. Common adverse reactions include burning, itching, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, hypopigmentation, allergic contact dermatitis, and secondary infections. For adult patients, hydrocortisone acetate suppositories are indicated for rectal administration. To use, detach one suppository from the strip, remove the wrapper, and avoid excessive handling as the suppository melts at body temperature. Insert the suppository into the rectum with gentle pressure, pointed end first. The typical dosage is one suppository twice daily (morning and night) for two weeks in nonspecific proctitis. In more severe cases, the dosage may be increased to one suppository three times daily or two suppositories twice daily. For factitial proctitis, therapy duration is typically six to eight weeks or less, depending on the individual response. There is limited information regarding off-label uses of hydrocortisone (rectal) in adults, as well as in pediatric patients. The drug label does not provide specific FDA guidance for pediatric indications, dosages, or off-label uses. Similarly, there is no FDA guidance for its use in geriatric populations, specific gender or racial groups, patients with renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised individuals. Hydrocortisone acetate suppositories are contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to hydrocortisone acetate or any of its components. Proctologic examination is recommended before use. If irritation develops, discontinue the product and initiate appropriate therapy. In the presence of an infection, antifungal or antibacterial agents should be used, and hydrocortisone acetate should be discontinued if a favorable response is not promptly observed. During pregnancy, hydrocortisone acetate suppositories should only be used if the potential benefit justifies the risk to the fetus. Topical steroids have been associated with fetal abnormalities in animal studies, and there are no adequate studies in pregnant women. The drug should not be used extensively, in large amounts, or for prolonged periods during pregnancy. It is unknown whether hydrocortisone acetate is excreted in human milk, so a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. Approximately 26% of hydrocortisone acetate is absorbed when applied rectally in normal subjects, with absorption potentially varying across abraded or inflamed surfaces. Topical steroids exert their effects primarily through anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions. Hydrocortisone acetate suppositories are off-white, smooth-surfaced, and rod-shaped with one pointed end. They are supplied in boxes of 12 or 24 suppositories. The product should be stored between 15°C and 30°C (59°F and 86°F) and protected from freezing. Federal law prohibits dispensing without a prescription. There is limited information regarding drug interactions, postmarketing experience, administration, monitoring, and IV compatibility for hydrocortisone (rectal). Additionally, there is no established interaction between alcohol and hydrocortisone (rectal), so patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication.
